newsitem.title: UK: British press chided over royal reports.
newsitem.headline: British press chided over royal reports.

text.p: The head of Britain's press watchdog commission on Wednesday chided newspapers for a spate of scandalous reports about the royal family and warned them they were undermining their right to self-regulation.

Lord Wakeham, chairman of the Press Complaints Commission, wrote to The Times newspaper on the day the Sun tabloid was forced to apologise to Princess Diana after it splashed its front page with stills from a hoax video it believed showed her cavorting with her former lover James Hewitt.
Events of the last few days had thrown into focus a matter that had been worrying him for some time, Wakeham said in the letter published in Thursday's edition of The Tines.

"Although these events concern primarily members and former members of the Royal Family, the key issues they raise -- invasion of privacy and the use of public interest defence by newspapers -- have wider ramifications," he said.

The effectiveness of self-regulation "is now in danger of being undermined because (of) a stream of injudicious stories centring on the private lives of public individuals, backed up only by the flimsiest of public interest defences."
Britain has resisted introducing privacy laws to curb the press but the threat of legislation has been raised repeatedly, usually following revelations about the royal family.
Royal supporters blamed the breakdown of the marriage of Princess Diana and heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles on the media, which revelled in reporting their marital troubles.
Diana's former sister-in-law the Duchess of York, better known as Fergie, has recently suffered a barrage of embarrassing press reports about her extra-marital affairs and financial troubles.
Wakeham said he was particularly concerned about the children of those involved, although he did not refer to any specific stories. Diana has two sons and Fergie two daughters.
"When a story breaks they (the children) are the first to suffer," he wrote.
"I can understand -- as could any parent -- why, in these circumstances, those individuals are reluctant to complain and perhaps prolong the suffering through the investigation."
He said the commission had the powers to carry out its own investigations "and would not hesitate to use them."
But he added that he did not believe legal controls were the way forward and urged newspapers not to bring the curbs down upon themselves.

"I therefore trust all those who have an interest in these issues will co-operate with me and with the Commission as we chart the way forward in strengthening self-regulation in this most difficult -- but critical -- of areas," he said.
